You are analyzing **one block of a longer dialogue** to extract actions.

**ACTION** = An atomic communicative act a speaker **directly performed** in a turn.
- Atomic action = minimal unit of action the speaker directly performed. - e.g.
"User asks to find a paper about HCI in NLP conferences" → split into "User asks
to find a paper about HCI", "User asks to find a paper in NLP conferences".
- Include evidence quote from the utterance.

**Possible action types** (generate new types if needed):
Accept, Acknowledge, Address, Allow, Analyze, Apologize, Ask, Challenge, Clarify,
Classify, Compare, Complain, Confirm, Connect, Constrain, Critique, Decide, Define,
Delegate, Describe, Draft, Emphasize, Evaluate, Explain, Feedback, Formalize, Frame,
Greet, Hypothesize, Implement, Include, Infer, Instruct, Invite, Justify, List,
Modify, Observe, Plan, Provide, Qualify, Recommend, Refuse, Report, Request, State,
Suggest, Summarize, Warn

**Role:** **SHAPER | EXECUTOR | OTHER**
* **SHAPER:** Creates/shapes/revises the goal/requirement by proposing new ideas,
new tasks, constraints, alternatives, or directions.
* **EXECUTOR:** Executes/achieves the desired outcome/goal/requirement (e.g.,
drafting text, providing requested information, coding, searching, implementing).
* **OTHER:** Neither SHAPER nor EXECUTOR.

**Turn ID format:** each turn is labeled **U(x,y)** or **A(x,y)**, where **U**=user
turn, **A**=AI turn, **x**=the pair number this turn belongs to (the 1st user+AI
exchange is pair 1, the 2nd is pair 2, etc.), and **y**=the action's position
within that turn (1, 2, 3… in the order it was extracted). e.g. the user's 2nd
atomic action in pair 1 is "U(1,2)"; the AI's 1st atomic action in pair 3 is
"A(3,1)". Use this format for every turn id below — do not use plain integers.

USER (this is the user turn of pair 6):
Okay, I decided to go with that disembodied paper, disembodied creativity in GenAI. But for this purpose, how should I read this? What is the approach to reading this? Because I don't know how to, what should my thinking process, how should I approach to read this and all, because I have not actually practiced papers before. So guide me on how to read this so we get the best output and I have all the inputs and what should I do. I don't want to spend much time and also based on my notes and my experiences and what all I have, how should I answer that three questions for tomorrow's presentation?

AI (this is the AI turn of pair 6):
Good question, and honest one. Reading an academic paper for the first time is a skill, not a talent — and the good news is you don't need to read it the way a PhD student would. You need to read it the way a Master's student preparing a 3-sentence verbal intro for Monday would. Those are very different jobs.

Here's how I'd approach it.

The mindset shift first

You're not reading to "understand every sentence." You're reading to extract three things: the core claim, two or three concepts that give you vocabulary, and a couple of memorable phrases you can quote or paraphrase confidently if asked a follow-up. That's it. If you try to read this as a textbook, you'll get lost in the Dreyfus references and Simondon's philosophy of technology and you'll walk in Monday overwhelmed instead of confident. Don't do that.

The paper is 9 pages. You need maybe 45 minutes with it tonight, done in two passes. Not more.

Pass one — the orientation pass (15 minutes)

Read only these parts, in this order:

Start with the abstract. It's on page 1, eight sentences long. Read it twice. The abstract is the paper's whole argument compressed — if you understand the abstract, you understand the paper's position. Everything else is supporting detail. After reading it twice, close your eyes and try to state in your own words what the authors are claiming. If you can't, read it a third time.

Then skip to the conclusion (Section 5, page 7–8, about half a page). The conclusion restates the abstract with a bit more nuance and tells you what the authors want you to take away. Read it once.

Then read the introduction (Section 1, about one page). The key move to watch for: the authors set up an opposing view — that generative AI is just another mediating tool like pencils or Photoshop — and then announce they will argue the opposite. That's the paper's rhetorical structure. Recognizing this will help you answer the "what is it about" question.

At this point, stop. Put the paper down. Walk around for two minutes. Let it settle.

After the break, ask yourself: If someone stopped me in the hallway and said "what's that paper about," could I answer in two sentences? If yes, you're ready for pass two. If no, reread the abstract once more.

Pass two — the concept-mining pass (25 minutes)

Now read the middle sections, but selectively. You do NOT need to read every paragraph. You're hunting for concepts you can name-drop if asked.

Section 1.1 and 1.2 (Modes of Existence of LLMs) — skim this. The key concept here is that LLMs are not autonomous agents; the authors call them "linguistic automata" or a "talking library." There's a technical term, "midtended agency," from Barandiaran & Almendros — you don't need to master it, just recognize it. One sentence worth of understanding is enough.

Section 2.1 (Creativity is an embodied process) — read this more carefully. This is the heart of the paper. The key names are Pallasmaa ("the thinking hand"), Sennett ("the craftsman"), and the general idea that creativity happens through the loop of mind, hand, and surroundings. The Frank Gehry example is memorable — an architect who feels something is wrong before he can articulate why, and this inarticulate-yet-knowing quality is what prompt-based AI can't access. If you remember one example from the paper, remember this one.

Section 2.2 (Creativity beyond discourse) — the Dreyfus five-stage model. You need to know this at a surface level: novice → advanced beginner → competent → proficient → expert. The argument is that prompt-based systems trap users at the novice stage forever, because prompting is rule-following, and rule-following is what experts have moved beyond. The bicycle metaphor is worth remembering: you can't learn to ride a bike by reading instructions, you have to fall off a few times. Same with creative work.

Section 2.3 (Not all mediating technologies are equal) — skim. The point is that digital tools like Illustrator already have some autocracy (the software makes choices for you), but GenAI is a much bigger leap because you lose even more control.

Section 3 (What creativity is and is not) — read the subsection headings and the first sentence of each. The authors argue against four claims made by GenAI proponents: that it democratizes creativity, that visuals are just pixels, that creativity benefits from scaling, that efficiency matters for creativity. You don't need to master each argument. Just know the structure.

Section 4 (Discussion) — read the "recapitulation" at 4.1. It's a numbered list of five points that summarizes everything. This is gold. If you understand those five numbered points, you understand the paper.

That's your read. You don't need to touch the references section.

What to write down as you read

Open a blank note or a piece of paper. As you read, jot down:

A one-sentence summary of the paper in your own words. Not the authors' words — yours. This forces comprehension.

Three concepts you could name if asked: I'd pick embodied / disembodied creativity, the Dreyfus five-stage skill model, and tacit knowledge (Polanyi). You don't need to explain them deeply. You just need to say the words without stumbling.

One memorable example: Frank Gehry feeling something is wrong before he can say why. Or the pencil-can't-carve-marble line from the introduction. Pick one that sticks in your head.

One honest reaction — what did you agree with, what did you find overreaching? Having a personal view matters more than you'd think. If Prof. von Maydell asks "what did you think of it," a confident "I agreed strongly with X but I think the authors overstated Y" is a much better answer than a summary.

Now, your three-sentence verbal intro

You asked how to answer the three questions using your notebook and your experience, not just the paper. This is the right instinct. Memorized answers sound canned. Personal ones land.

Here's how I'd approach each question, with the personal layer woven in.

Question 1 — Why is this paper important for the course (how does it tackle GenAI in creativity)?

The course is about generative AI and creativity. Most GenAI discourse celebrates democratization — anyone can now make images, films, music. This paper takes the opposite position: that the dominant interaction paradigm, prompting, is fundamentally mismatched with how creative expertise actually develops. That's a disagreement worth taking seriously in a course like this, because if the authors are right, the current wave of creative AI tools isn't empowering creators, it's producing a generation of perpetual novices. That's the contribution.

Your personal angle: you can say "this paper articulates something I've been feeling in my own practice." You don't need to share the whole deskilling story from your notebook — just one concrete line. Something like: "I've noticed in my own work with AI that I'm often producing more, faster, but I'm not developing the skills I thought I was building."

Question 2 — What is the paper about?

Two sentences max. First sentence: the core claim. Second sentence: the reasoning.

Try something like: "The authors argue that prompt-based generative AI produces a fundamentally different kind of creativity than traditional or even digital creative practice — one that is disembodied, rule-based, and traps users at a novice level of engagement. They draw on philosophy of expertise and embodied cognition to argue that tacit creative knowledge — the kind expert painters, architects, or filmmakers develop through years of hands-on work — can't be externalized into text prompts, which means prompt-based tools can never support genuine skill development."

That's it. Don't over-explain.

Question 3 — Where was it published, and by whom?

Short and confident: "It was published in Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence in August 2025, by David Casacuberta of the Universitat Autònoma de Barcelona and Ariel Guersenzvaig of the Elisava School of Design in Barcelona. Both are philosophers of design." That's enough. If asked why a journal and not a conference, your honest answer is: "The assignment listed Google Scholar as one of the valid sources, and I searched there because I was looking for a paper that took a philosophical position on prompt-based AI rather than a systems paper. This one fit my interest more precisely than anything I found in the SIGCHI venues."

A few tactical notes for tomorrow

Don't try to memorize a script. Memorize the structure — three beats, roughly a sentence each — and let the phrasing come naturally. If you memorize verbatim and forget a word, you'll freeze. If you know the shape, you can rebuild it live.

Print the paper, or at least have it on a screen you can flip to. If Prof. von Maydell asks about a specific section, you want to be able to turn to it rather than trying to recall from memory.

If you're asked something you don't know, say so. "I didn't go that deep into section X, but my understanding at a high level is…" is a completely acceptable answer for a Master's-level seminar. Faking knowledge of Dreyfus's full phenomenology when you've only read one summary will backfire.

Finally — and this is the one thing most students miss — the professor isn't trying to catch you out. He's trying to see if you can engage with a paper thoughtfully. A confident, personal, honest response to a paper you've read carefully for 45 minutes is worth more than a rehearsed summary of a paper you've read for 4 hours. Read it once with attention, write down your own reaction, and walk in trusting yourself.

That's the whole approach. Tonight: 45 minutes, two passes, one page of notes. Tomorrow: three sentences, structured not scripted, with one personal line woven in. You'll be fine.
